analysis.one_liner: Strengthens workers' right to unionize, strike, and bargain, and sharply raises penalties on employers who violate labor law.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 224-194 in February 2020, but the Senate never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites federal labor law to make it easier for workers to join unions and harder for employers to stop them. It bans mandatory anti-union meetings, allows secondary strikes, overrides state right-to-work laws, bans forced-arbitration agreements that block workers from joining class actions, and raises fines for companies that fire or retaliate against workers who organize. The House passed it with a near party-line vote; the Senate never voted on it, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to organize a union get stronger protections: employers could no longer fire or replace them for striking, force them into anti-union meetings, or make them sign away their right to join class-action lawsuits [S4]. Workers misclassified as independent contractors would be covered by labor law under a stricter test [S5]. Union members in the roughly half of states with right-to-work laws could be covered by collective-bargaining agreements requiring fee contributions from everyone the union represents [S4][S5]. Whistleblowers who report labor-law violations get new protections [S5].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unfair labor practice to replace or discriminate against workers who participate in strikes, and to require or coerce employees to attend employer meetings designed to discourage union membership [S4].
Lets collective-bargaining agreements require all employees in a bargaining unit to pay fees for representation, overriding state right-to-work laws [S4][S5].
Prohibits employers from enforcing agreements that make workers give up the right to pursue joint, class, or collective claims, overriding forced-arbitration arrangements [S5].

Raises the stakes for violations: civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation, doubled to $100,000 for repeat offenders, plus back pay without reductions, two times liquidated damages, and a private right of action allowing workers to sue in federal court [S5].

Speeds up union elections by setting firm timelines, requires employers to provide voter lists to the union, and bars employers from participating in the representation proceedings themselves [S4][S5].

For first contracts, if bargaining and mediation fail after about 120 days, a tripartite arbitration panel imposes a binding two-year agreement so a newly certified union cannot be stalled indefinitely [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on keeping workplaces union-free bear the cost: higher fines, litigation exposure, and disclosure of paid anti-union consultants [S4][S5]. The union-avoidance consulting industry loses business as the bill narrows the exemption for anti-union 'persuader' arrangements [S4]. Arbitration providers lose forced-arbitration agreements [S5]. Franchisors and temp-staffing firms face joint-employer liability when they share control over workers' conditions [S5]. App-based gig platforms face a stricter test that could reclassify contractors as employees [S5].

drawbacks.text: By overriding state right-to-work laws, the bill lets collective-bargaining agreements require fees from workers in the unit even if they choose not to join the union [S4][S5].
First-contract arbitration lets a government-facilitated panel impose a binding two-year contract on both the union and the employer, even if one side rejects the terms [S5].
The bill bars employers from participating in any National Labor Relations Board representation proceeding, which critics called a denial of due process for the party facing the election [S4][S5].
Expanded penalties, double damages, and a private right of action raise litigation costs for employers of all sizes, including small businesses that could face $50,000-per-violation exposure [S5].
Legalizing secondary strikes allows unions to pressure companies that are not directly in a dispute with their own workers, pulling neutral third parties into labor conflicts [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the bill substantially strengthens rights that are hard to enforce today: union election timelines, strike protection, and real financial penalties. The costs fall on employers, concentrated in those with anti-union practices, though honest supporters should acknowledge that small businesses face higher litigation exposure and that workers in right-to-work states who decline union membership could be compelled to pay representation fees. The due-process objection to excluding employers from election proceedings is a real design concern, not just industry talking points.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in February 2020, but the Senate referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never voted on it; it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 2, 2019 and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S1][S7].
It drew 218 cosponsors, 216 of them House Democrats and 2 Republicans [S6].
The committee reported the bill as amended on a 26-21 vote in September 2019 [S7].
The House passed it 224-194 on February 6, 2020: 219 Democrats and 5 Republicans voted yes, while 186 Republicans and 7 Democrats voted no [S9].

The Senate received the bill on February 10, 2020 and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; the record shows no further Senate action for the rest of the 116th Congress [S1][S7].
Before passage, a Republican motion to recommit with an amendment barring unions from communicating with workers not authorized to work in the United States failed 195-223 [S8].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on keeping workplaces union-free, along with the anti-union consulting and forced-arbitration industries, are better off because the bill never became law. No senator was ever required to cast a recorded vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost entirely by party: 219 Democrats voted yes and 7 no, while 5 Republicans voted yes and 186 no [S9].

industries.industry: Anti-union consulting firms and management-side labor law firms
industries.note: The bill bans mandatory captive-audience anti-union meetings and narrows the reporting exemption for paid consultants hired to persuade employees not to organize, shrinking their core business. Their income depends on keeping workers unorganized, which runs directly against the workers' interests [S4][S5].

The bill's stricter contractor test (control, outside the usual course of the business, independently established trade) could reclassify many gig workers as employees covered by labor law. Platforms' business model relies on contractor status; some workers on these platforms prefer the flexibility of contractor status.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and employers using forced-arbitration agreements
industries.note: The bill voids agreements that make employees give up the right to join class or collective actions over employment disputes, a common practice upheld by the Supreme Court in recent years. Employers lose a tool that has kept many wage and workplace claims out of court.

A broadened joint-employer definition holds companies liable when they share or indirectly control workers' essential conditions of employment, reaching arrangements designed to keep the formal employer at arm's length. These structures exist largely to avoid bargaining obligations.

The bill expands unions' organizing tools (quick elections, employer exclusion from proceedings, secondary strikes, first-contract arbitration) and makes fair-share fees enforceable nationwide. Union strength in bargaining is the vehicle through which workers would capture the bill's gains.

Unionized and organizing employers face penalties up to $100,000 per violation, double damages, and private lawsuits, while employers whose workers simply stay non-union without violations face little direct cost. The compliance burden falls hardest on those with the most violations.
